passage: Each September, Arctic sea ice contracts to its annual minimum before refreezing through the winter. Drawing on satellite records compiled by the National Snow and Ice Data Center, climatologists have argued that the most extreme low-ice years in the Arctic record have grown anomalous faster than typical years have, meaning that decadal extremes are pulling away from decadal averages rather than declining in step with them because _______

questionTable.caption: Mean September Arctic sea ice extent and lowest single-year extent, by decade, 1980-2020 (National Snow and Ice Data Center)

question: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.text: the decadal mean September extent declined in every decade shown, moving from 7.2 million km² in the 1980s to 6.6 in the 1990s, 5.8 in the 2000s, and 4.6 in the 2010s.
between the 1980s and the 2010s the decadal lows fell from 6.9 to 3.6 million km², a drop of 3.3 million km², while the decadal means fell from 7.2 to 4.6 million km², a drop of only 2.6 million km².
the lowest single year on record, 3.6 million km² in 2012, represented roughly half the 1980s decadal mean of 7.2 million km², a reduction of about 50 percent across the period.
the decadal means dropped by 2.6 million km² between the 1980s and the 2010s, while the decadal lows fell by only 3.3 million km² over the same span, a smaller change in the extreme years.

explanation: The claim is comparative and very specific: decadal extremes (the lowest single year in each decade) have pulled AWAY from decadal averages — that is, the lows have fallen FASTER than the means. To support that claim, the choice has to put the two columns of the table side by side and show that the change in the 'lowest year' column exceeds the change in the 'mean' column. Choice B does exactly this: the lows dropped 3.3 million km² (6.9 → 3.6) and the means dropped 2.6 million km² (7.2 → 4.6), and 3.3 > 2.6, so the extremes did fall faster. Both numbers are read straight from the table; both halves of the comparison are present; and the direction of the comparison matches the claim.
